snippet.title: How did ancient civilizations brew beer? - Malcolm Purinton
snippet.description:
Trace the history and evolution of beer, from its first known existence 13,000 years ago to the modern beverage we know today.

--

Today, there are over 100 distinct beer varieties, from pilsners and bocks, to porters, stouts, and IPAs. The oldest evidence of beer brewing dates back 13,000 years, but experts believe the drink developed independently across the world. So, how did ancient civilizations brew beer, and how did their methods develop into the beverage we know today? Malcolm Purinton traces the evolution of beer.

Lesson Malcolm Purinton, directed by Anton Bogaty.

snippet.title: The election of George Washington was weirder than you think
snippet.description:
The first U.S. presidential election in 1789 had none of the features Americans associate with elections today: no campaigning for the office, no political parties or conventions, no primary elections. Election Day was in January rather than November. The Electoral College was taken seriously rather than being treated as a formality. This was the only election in which a state was disqualified from participating. And there was only one issue at stake: whether the Constitution itself should be scrapped.

The final results of the election were that George Washington received 69 electoral votes and John Adams 34, making them president and vice president, respectively. John Adams should have received at least 49 votes, but many of the electors who wanted to vote for him voted for other people instead because of a scheme that Alexander Hamilton helped create. So instead of Adams receiving 71% of the electoral vote as he would have, he only received 49%.

snippet.title: How a broken heart affects your body - Roni Shanoada
snippet.description:
Dig into broken heart syndrome, and find out how grief and traumatic events can affect your body and health.

--


Losing a loved one can be one of the most traumatic experiences of a person’s life. Grief brings on a whole host of strong emotions that impact both our mental and physical health. But is it possible for these powerful feelings to endanger your life? In other words, can you actually die from a broken heart? Roni Shanoada explores how traumatic events can affect your body.

Lesson by Roni Shanoada, directed by Joana Sus, NOMINT.

snippet.title: Why British Aristocrats Are Purposely Letting Their Estates Go Wild
snippet.description:
The British countryside is hiding a dark truth, having lost half of its native plant and animal species since the industrial revolution. For centuries, intensive human intervention, aggressive farming, and relentless drainage systems stripped the land of its natural identity. Now, an elite group of historic estates and aristocratic landowners are launching a radical operation to surrender control back to the wild. This documentary takes you behind the closed gates of Mapperton House, Elmore Court, and Castle Howard to witness the high-stakes battle for ecological restoration. As the merchant classes became a thing, in the later Middle Ages, funerals developed into public displays of wealth. Not just the act of burial itself, but also the broadcasting of a death to the whole community. The men who walked the streets, ringing bells and announcing a bereavement were known as the Criers of the Dead. 

Lets travel back in time and take a look at how their job evolved, as did the medieval funeral until it became a dramatic spectacle of hand wringing, hair pulling, chest beating, crying and wailing. snippet.title: The Rise and Fall of the Vikings | Why the Most Feared Warriors in History Vanished
snippet.description:
For centuries, the Vikings struck fear across Europe raiding coasts, exploring new lands, and building a reputation as some of the most formidable warriors in history. But over time, their dominance faded.

In this video, we explore the rise, expansion, and eventual decline of the Viking world, and what really caused their disappearance as a major force.

You’ll Discover:
How Viking society and seafaring skills fueled their rapid expansion
The role of trade, exploration, and settlement beyond raiding
Why European defenses and kingdoms became harder to attack
The impact of Christianization and cultural change
How political shifts and integration led to the end of the Viking Age

The Vikings didn’t just vanish overnight they evolved, settled, and became part of the societies they once raided.

Sometimes the end of an era… isn’t destruction, but transformation.

snippet.title: What Mary II and William III Used To Eat | Life Inside Kensington Palace (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
The real lives of King William III and Queen Mary II had nothing to do with the polished portraits hanging in their palaces. This documentary pulls back the curtain on what they actually ate, where they truly slept, how they bathed, and what daily life looked like inside Kensington Palace and Hampton Court in the late 1600s. From salted herring and secret chocolate kitchens to chamber pots and linen-based hygiene, the truth is far more fascinating than the history books admit.

Lessons Covered in this video:

The Chocolate Kitchens at Hampton Court were built by Christopher Wren around 1690 and lost for centuries, only rediscovered in 2013
Mary II loved oranges so deeply she had an entire Orangery built at Hampton Court to house her citrus trees
Both William and Mary drank chocolate as a hot beverage every morning — a luxury item at the time
William and Mary's Kitchen Garden at Hampton Court, built in 1689, fed the royal court for over 160 years

snippet.title: Persia or Iran? Farsi or Persian? Which one is right?
snippet.description:
The country of Iran used to be called Persia. Who changed its name and why? Also is the language of Iran Persian or Farsi? Is it okay to say "Persian"? Where do the words "Persian" and "Farsi" come from? 

I answer all these questions in this video.

EDIT: Many Iranians are discovering this video (Welcome! Khosh amadid!), and some are upset by what I say here. I recommend they read this piece by Ehsan Yarshater, a distinguished scholar of Persian/Iranian history:
https://web.archive.org/web/20160714205848/http://www.iran-heritage.org/interestgroups/language-article5.htm

N.B.: Don't think that because some Iranians/Persians in the comments are objecting to the terms "Persia" and "Persian", that that represents all people of Iran or of Persian culture. Many Persians would prefer that Westerners use the term "Persian." Some prominent ones are named in the short article linked above, and I have also known Persians in my daily life who expressed this view. When Reza Shah issued that request to foreign governments in 1934, he created an unnecessary complication that makes it more difficult for foreigners to get to know and understand the Persian people.

Sources for my claim that Reza Shah's request was a 'marketing gimmick':

"The most visible name change came in 1934 when Reza Shah -- prompted by his legation in Berlin -- decreed that henceforth Persia was to be known to the outside world as Iran. A government circular explained that whereas "Persia" was associated with Fars and Qajar decadence, "Iran" invoked the glories and birthplace of the ancient Aryans." 
Ervand Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (Cambridge, 2009), page 86

"In terms of foreign policy, Reza Shah was determined to maintain Iran's independence and to restore its sense of national pride by elevating its stature in the world and insisting it be treated with respect. This was the motivation behind any number of his actions, from insisting on the use of the name Iran instead of Persia to banning photographs of things that were picturesque but might give an impression of backwardness (camels, for example) to breaking off diplomatic relations with countries if its newspapers published unflattering articles about him or his country."
Elton L. Daniel, The History of Iran (Greenwood Press, 2001), pages 139-140
